**Surah al-Mu'min (The Believer)**

Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: It is also called Surah al-Tawl. It is Meccan, as stated by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, and Qatadah. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah that two of its verses were revealed in Medina: His saying ﴿Those who dispute concerning the signs of Allah﴾ and the one after it [40:35, 40:36]. Al-Zajjaj said: It is mentioned that all the Hawamim (the surahs beginning with Ha Mim) were revealed in Mecca.

Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said that "Ha Mim" is one of the names of Allah, and this surah was attributed to it, as if it were said: "the surah of Allah," for its nobility and excellence. So it was called "Al Ha Mim," although the whole Qur'an is the surahs of Allah. This is like saying "the House of Allah," "the Sanctuary of Allah," and "the she-camel of Allah." al-Kumayt said:

*We found for you in the family of Ha Mim a sign,*
*which a pious one among us interpreted, and an Arabized one.*

"Ha Mim" may also be used as the name of the surah, and it takes inflection (i'rab) and is not diptotic (la yusraf). Whoever says this of all of them says "al-Hawamim," as one says "Ta Sin" and "al-Tawasin." Muhammad ibn al-Qasim al-Anbari said: The Arabs say: "He fell upon the Hawamim" and "in the family of Ha Mim." Abu 'Ubaydah recited:

*I swear by the seven that were lengthened,*
*and by the hundreds (mi'in) that came after them and were made to be counted (umi'it),*

*and by the mathani that were doubled and repeated,*
*and by the Tawasin that were made threefold,*

*and by the Hawamim that were made sevens,*
*and by the Mufassal that were detailed.*

Whoever says "he fell upon the family of Ha Mim" makes "Ha Mim" the name of all of them. Whoever says "he fell upon the Hawamim" makes "Ha Mim" like a single letter, like Qabil and Habil. I read to our shaykh Abu Mansur al-Lughawi, who said: It is an error to say "I read the Hawamim," and it is not in the speech of the Arabs; the correct form is to say "I read the family of Ha Mim." In a hadith of Ibn Mas'ud: "When it falls in the family of Ha Mim, it falls in gardens, soft and sweet-smelling."

Regarding ﴿Ha Mim﴾ there are four opinions.

The first: It is an oath which Allah swore by, and it is one of His names, azza wa jall. This is narrated by Ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn 'Abbas. Abu Sulayman said: It has been said that the answer to the oath is His saying ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved will be called out to﴾ [40:10].

The second: They are letters from the names of Allah, azza wa jall. Within this there are three opinions. The first: that "Alif Lam Ra," "Ha Mim," and "Nun" are letters of "al-Rahman" (the Most Merciful); this is narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: that the Ha is the key to His name "Hamid" (the Praiseworthy), and the Mim is the key to His name "Majid" (the Glorious); this was said by Abu al-'Aliyah. The third: that the Ha is the key to every name of Allah that begins with Ha, such as "Hakim," "Halim," and "Hayy," and the Mim is the key to every name that begins with Mim, such as "Malik," "Mutakabbir," and "Majid." This was related by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi, and something similar was narrated from 'Ata' al-Khurasani.

The third: The meaning of "Ha Mim" is: what is to occur has been decreed. This is narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The like of this is narrated from al-Dahhak and al-Kisa'i, as if they intended a reference to "Hamm" (with the Ha vowelled with a damma and the Mim doubled). Al-Zajjaj said: It has been said regarding "Ha Mim": "Humma al-amr" (the matter has been decreed).

The fourth: That "Ha Mim" is one of the names of the Qur'an; this was said by Qatadah.

Ibn Kathir recited "Ha Mim" with a fatha on the Ha. Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i recited it with a kasra on it. The reading of the rest differs. Al-Zajjaj said: As for the Mim, it is sakin (unvowelled) in the recitation of all the readers except 'Isa ibn 'Umar, who made it fatha. The fatha is of two kinds. The first: that one makes "Ha Mim" the name of the surah, so that it is in the accusative and is not given tanwin, because it follows the pattern of foreign names, like Habil and Qabil. The second: according to the meaning "recite Ha Mim." The better view is that the fatha is due to the meeting of two unvowelled letters, when one makes it the name of the surah, and it is the transmission of the letters of the alphabet.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The revelation of the Book﴾, meaning: this is the revelation of the Book. "Al-Tawb" is the plural of "tawbah" (repentance), and it is permissible that it be a verbal noun from "taba yatubu tawban." "Al-Tawl" is favour. Abu 'Ubaydah said: It is said: "So-and-so has favour (tawl) over his people," meaning: he has excellence. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said: "Tull 'alayya, may Allah have mercy on you," meaning: "be gracious to me." Al-Khattabi said: "Dhu" is the particle of relation (harf al-nisbah). Relation in their speech takes three forms: with the yā' (ya), as in "asadiyy" and "bikriyy"; the second is by the plural, as in "al-mahalibah," "al-masami'ah," and "al-azariqah"; and the third is with "dhi" and "dhat," as in their saying "rajul mal" (a man of wealth), meaning "dhu mal"; "kabsh safin" (a ram of wool), meaning "dhu suf"; and "naqah damir" (a lean she-camel), meaning "dhat damr." So His saying ﴿Dhu al-Tawl﴾ means: the people of favour and excellence.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 40, verses 4–6:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿None dispute concerning the signs of Allah except those who disbelieve﴾. That is: none contend regarding them by denying them and repelling them with falsehood. The rest of the verse is in [Ali 'Imran: 196]. The meaning is: the outcome of their affair is toward punishment, like the outcome of those before them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And every nation plotted against their messenger to seize him﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: to kill him, said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah. The second: to imprison him and torture him; and the captive is called akhidh (captive), related by Ibn Qutaybah. Al-Akhfash said: He said "li-ya'khudhuhu" (to seize him) in the plural, because "kull" (every) is masculine in form while its meaning is that of a group. What follows this is explained in [al-Kahf: 56], up to His saying: ﴿So I seized them﴾, meaning: I punished them and destroyed them. (p-208) ﴿So how was My punishment?﴾ This is a rhetorical question affirming the punishment that befell them. ﴿And thus﴾, meaning: just as what was decreed against the disbelieving nations ﴿the word of your Lord was fulfilled﴾ with punishment, which is His saying: ﴿I will surely fill Hell﴾ [al-A'raf: 18], upon those of your people who disbelieved. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited: (ḥaqqat kalimāt rabbika) "the words of your Lord were fulfilled." ﴿That they﴾. Al-Akhfash said: because they, or that they, ﴿are the companions of the Fire﴾.

Then he mentioned the merit of the believers, saying: ﴿Those who bear the Throne﴾. They are four angels, and on the Day of Resurrection they will be made eight. ﴿And those around it﴾. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Around the Throne there are seventy thousand rows of angels who circle it, and behind them are a hundred thousand rows of angels. Among them there is no one who does not glorify God with something other than what the others glorify Him with. Others said: Those around the Throne are the Karubiyyun (the cherubim, the foremost of the angels), and they are the chiefs of the angels. We have already explained in the previous surah the meaning of His words: ﴿They glorify their Lord with His praise﴾ [al-Zumar: 75].

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 40, verse 10–12:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieved will be called out to: The hatred of Allah [toward you] is greater than your hatred of yourselves, when you were being invited to the faith but you disbelieved.﴾ The exegetes said: When they saw their deeds and were made to enter the Fire, they hated themselves for the evil of their actions. Then a caller calls out to them: The hatred of Allah toward you in the world ﴿when you were invited to faith but you disbelieved﴾ is greater than your hatred of yourselves.

Then He informed of what they say in the Fire, with His words: ﴿Our Lord, You have caused us to die twice and You have given us life twice.﴾ This is like His words: ﴿How can you disbelieve in Allah when you were dead and He gave you life? Then He will cause you to die, then He will bring you to life, then to Him you will be returned.﴾ [al-Baqarah: 28]. We have explained it there.

[p. 210] **He it is who shows you His signs** means His creations, which point to His oneness (tawhid, the affirmation of God's unity) and His power. Here "provision" (rizq) means rain. It was called provision because it is the cause of sustenance. "Takes heed" (yatadhakkaru) means takes admonition, and "turns back" (yunib) means returns to obedience.

Then He commanded the believers to affirm His oneness, saying: **So call upon Allah, sincere to Him in religion.** That is, affirming His oneness.

His saying, the Exalted: **Raised in degrees.** Ibn Abbas said: it means raising the heavens. Al-Mawardi related from some exegetes that he said: its meaning is "Great in attributes."

His saying, the Exalted: **Lord of the Throne.** That is, its Creator and Owner.

His saying, the Exalted: **He casts the Spirit.** Regarding this there are five opinions.

The first is that it is the Qur'an. The second is prophethood. Both opinions are narrated from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Zayd said the first, and al-Suddi said the second. The third is revelation (wahy), said by Qatada. The Qur'an and revelation were called "spirit" because the religion is sustained by them, just as the body is sustained by the spirit. The fourth is Jibril (Gabriel), said by al-Dahhak. The fifth is mercy, related by Ibrahim al-Harbi.

His saying, the Exalted: **upon whomever He wills of His servants.** That is, the prophets.

**That he may warn.** Regarding the one referred to, there are two opinions. The first is that it is Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. The second is the prophet to whom revelation is sent.

What is meant by **the Day of Meeting** is the Day of Resurrection. Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub retained the "ya'" in "al-taladi" in both pause and continuation, and Abu Ja'far agreed with them in continuation; the rest omitted the "ya'" in both states. Regarding the reason for it being named thus, there are five opinions.

The first: the people of the heavens and the earth meet on it, narrated by Yusuf ibn Mihran from Ibn Abbas.

The second: the first and last generations meet on it, also narrated from Ibn Abbas.

The third: [the creation meets] the Creator on it, said by Qatada and Muqatil.

The fourth: the oppressed and the oppressor meet on it, said by Maymun ibn Mihran.

The fifth: a person meets his deed on it, related by al-Tha'labi.

His saying, the Exalted: **The Day they will come forth.** That is, they will be visible, coming out of their graves. **Nothing of them is hidden from Allah.**

If it is said: Is anything of them hidden from Him today?

The answer: No. However, the meaning of the statement is a warning of recompense. The exegetes have three opinions on this.

The first: nothing of what they did is hidden from Him. Said by Ibn Abbas. The second: [p. 212] they cannot hide from Him behind a mountain or a clod of earth, said by Qatada. The third: the meaning is that He will have brought them all forth, since nothing of them is hidden from Him, related by al-Mawardi.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 40, verses 18–19:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And warn them of the Imminent Day﴾, concerning which there are two opinions.

The first: it is the Day of Resurrection, as stated by the majority. Ibn Qutaybah said: The Resurrection was named thus because of its nearness; it is said: "The departure of so-and-so drew near" (azifa shukhus fulan), meaning: he drew near.

The second: it is the day of the arrival of death (al-maniyyah), as stated by Qutrub.

(p-213) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the hearts are at the throats, choking (with grief)﴾. This is because they rise up to the throats and neither leave nor return; this is according to the first opinion. According to the second: the hearts are the souls, reaching the throats at the arrival of death. Al-Zajjaj said: ﴿Choking﴾ (kazimin) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal), and the state is construed according to the meaning, since it is not said of hearts that they are "choking"; rather, it is those who possess the hearts who are choking. So the meaning is: when the hearts of people are at their throats while they are in a state of suppressed distress. The exegetes said: "Kazimin" means: distressed, filled with fear and sorrow; and the kazim is one who holds something in upon what is in it. We have already pointed to this at His saying: ﴿And those who restrain their anger﴾ [Al 'Imran: 134].

﴿For the wrongdoers﴾, meaning the disbelievers, ﴿there is no intimate friend (hamim) who will benefit them﴾, that is, a close relative who helps them, ﴿nor an intercessor who is obeyed﴾ on their behalf, so that his intercession would be accepted.

﴿He knows the treachery of the eyes﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: "Al-khaʼina" and "al-khiyana" are one and the same. The exegetes have four opinions regarding it.

The first: it is a man who is among a people when a woman passes by him; he shows them that he lowers his gaze, but when he sees a moment of heedlessness from them, he glances at her, and if he fears they will notice him, he lowers his gaze again. This was said by Ibn ʻAbbas.

The second: it is the gaze of the eye at what has been forbidden, said by Mujahid.

The third: it is winking with the eye, said by al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. Qatadah said: It is winking with the eye in what Allah does not love and does not approve.

The fourth: it is a glance after a glance, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what the breasts conceal﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions. The first: what one conceals of action, were you able to do what you looked at, said by Ibn ʻAbbas. The second: the whispering (al-waswasah), said by al-Suddi. The third: what the heart harbours of trustworthiness or treachery, related by al-Mawardi.

The first: it is a man who is among a people when a woman passes by him; he shows them that he lowers his gaze, but when he sees a moment of heedlessness from them, he glances at her, and if he fears they will notice him, he lowers his gaze again. This was said by Ibn ʻAbbas.

The second: it is the gaze of the eye at what has been forbidden, said by Mujahid.

The third: it is winking with the eye, said by al-Dahhak and al-Suddi. Qatadah said: It is winking with the eye in what Allah does not love and does not approve.

The fourth: it is a glance after a glance, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what the breasts conceal﴾. Concerning it there are three opinions. The first: what one conceals of action, were you able to do what you looked at, said by Ibn ʻAbbas. The second: the whispering (al-waswasah), said by al-Suddi. The third: what the heart harbours of trustworthiness or treachery, related by al-Mawardi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Allah judges with truth﴾, meaning He rules by it, so He recompenses with good and evil. ﴿And those whom they call upon besides Him﴾, meaning the deities. Nafi' and Ibn Amir read "تَدَّعُونَ" (tad-da-'-oon, "you call upon") with the letter ta', on the meaning: say to them, ﴿They do not judge anything﴾, meaning they do not rule over anything and do not recompense by it. By this, Allah, mighty and majestic, has drawn attention to the fact that He is living, because only one who is living commands and judges. He confirmed this by mentioning hearing and sight, because these are established only for a living being, as Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said. Part of what follows has already been covered [Yusuf: 109], and part is clear, up to His saying: ﴿They were stronger than them in power﴾. Ibn Amir read "أشَدُّ مِنكُمْ" (ashaddu minkum, "stronger than you") with the kaf, and it is likewise written so in their copies (maṣāḥif). This is a shift from the third person to the second person address. ﴿And they had no protector from Allah﴾, meaning from the punishment of Allah, ﴿against it﴾, meaning the punishment did not leave them.

﴿That﴾, meaning that punishment which befell them, ﴿is because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs . . .﴾ to the end of the verse.

Then He mentioned the story of Musa and Fir'awn so that they might take heed. By His saying: ﴿Kill the sons of those who believe with him﴾, he intended: reinstate the killing against them as it was at first. This was said by Ibn Abbas. Qatadah said: Fir'awn had stopped killing the boys, but when Allah sent Musa, he resumed the killing against them, to deter them thereby from following Musa.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the plot of the disbelievers is nothing but in error﴾, meaning it will go in vain, and what Allah, mighty and majestic, intends will overtake them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 40, verses 26–34:

﴿And Pharaoh said, "Leave me to kill Moses."﴾ He only said this because among Pharaoh's close associates there were those who would prevent him from killing Moses, out of fear of destruction. ﴿And let him call upon his Lord﴾, the one whom he claims has sent him; let Him protect him from being killed. ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾, meaning your worship of me, ( ﴿and that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾ ). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "wa-an" without an alif. 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "aw an" with an alif before the waw, meaning: if he does not change your religion, he will cause corruption. However, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "yuzhira" with a damma on the yā' and "al-fasad" in the accusative (naṣb). The rest read "yazhara" with a fatha on the yā' and "al-fasadu" in the nominative (raf'). The meaning is: corruption will appear through the alteration of our laws, so he deemed that corruption according to his own claim. It was also said: he will kill your sons as you do to them.

When Pharaoh said this, Moses sought refuge with his Lord, and said: ﴿Indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord﴾. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "'udtu" with the dhāl clearly pronounced; Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf assimilated it (idghām). ﴿From every arrogant one﴾, meaning one who is too proud to believe. Pharaoh then intended to kill Moses, and at that point ﴿a man of faith from the family of Pharaoh said...﴾ [p. 217] There are two opinions regarding "al" (family) here.

The first: it means relatives and kin. As-Suddi and Muqatil said: he was a cousin of Pharaoh, and this is the one meant by the words: ﴿And there came a man from the farthest end of the city, running﴾ [al-Qasas: 20].

The second: it means clan and tribe. Qatadah and Muqatil said: he was a Copt. Some said: he was an Israelite, and the meaning is only: a man of faith who concealed his faith from the family of Pharaoh. Regarding his name there are five opinions.

The first: Hizbil, said by Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. The second: Habib, said by Ka'b. The third: Sam'un, with an unpointed sīn, said by Shu'ayb al-Jiba'i. The fourth: Jibril (Gabriel). The fifth: Sham'an, with a pointed shīn, related from Ibn Ishaq; al-Zajjaj also related it as "Sham'an" with a shīn, and Ibn Makula mentioned it with a pointed shīn as well. Most scholars hold that he believed in Moses when Moses came. al-Hasan said: he was a believer before Moses came, and so was Pharaoh's wife. Muqatil said: he concealed his faith from Pharaoh for a hundred years.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Will you kill a man merely because he says, "My Lord is Allah"?﴾ That is, because he says ﴿"My Lord is Allah"﴾. This is a rhetorical question of denunciation. ﴿And he has certainly brought you clear proofs﴾, that is, things that indicate his truthfulness. ﴿And if he is a liar, upon him is his lie﴾, that is, that will not harm you. ﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾ of punishment. Regarding "some" (ba'd) there are three opinions.

[p. 218] The first: it means "all"; this was said by Abu 'Ubaydah, who cited the verse of Labid:

"Abandoner of dwelling places when I do not find them pleasing, or when some souls are seized by their death..."

He meant: all souls.

The second: it is redundant (ṣilah), and the meaning is: what he promises you will befall you. This is related from al-Layth.

The third: it retains its original sense, and there are two views on this. One: he promised them salvation if they believed and destruction if they disbelieved, so mention of "some" was used because they would be in one of the two states. The second: he promised them destruction in this world and punishment in the Hereafter for their disbelief, so their destruction in this world became part of the promise. Both are mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Al-Zajjaj said: this is a method of reasoning in which the debater binds the opponent to the proof using the least demanding aspect of the matter, and this does not negate that all of it will befall them. A similar statement is the poet's:

"The one who takes his time may attain some of his need, and the hasty one may well stumble."

The poet mentioned "some" only to imply the whole, because "some" is part of the whole. But when the speaker says: the least that the patient one gains is attaining some of his need, and the least that the hasty one gets is stumbling, he has shown the superiority of the patient over the hasty by something the opponent cannot refute. Thus the believer was saying to them: at the very least, in his truthfulness, some of what he promises you will befall you, and in some of that is your destruction. He said: as for Labid's verse, he meant by "some souls" only his own soul.

[p. 219] His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide﴾, that is, does not grant success to what is right, ﴿one who is a transgressor﴾. There are two opinions regarding this. The first: he is the polytheist, said by Qatadah. The second: he is one who sheds blood unlawfully, said by Mujahid.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Dominant in the land﴾, that is, exalted in the land of Egypt. ﴿So who will help us﴾, that is, who will protect us ﴿against the might of Allah﴾, that is, against His punishment. The meaning is: do not expose yourselves to punishment by denying him and killing the Prophet. At that point Pharaoh said: ﴿I show you only what I see﴾ of opinion and advice ﴿and I guide you only to the path of right conduct﴾, that is, I call you only to the way of guidance in denying Moses and believing in me. This indicates that he fell silent in response to the believer.

﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the day of the factions"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, like the day of the faction of the factions; the meaning is: I fear that if you persist in your disbelief, punishment will come upon you like what befell the nations that denied their messengers.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿The day of calling out﴾. 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "al-tanad" without a yā'. Ibn Kathir and Ya'qub read it with the yā' both in continuous recitation and at pause; Abu Ja'far agreed with them in continuous recitation. Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Jubayr, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak read "al-tannaddu" with the dhāl shaddah. Al-Zajjaj said: as for keeping the yā', that is the original form, and omitting it is good and fine, [p. 220] because the kasra indicates the yā', and it is the end of the verse, and the endings of these verses rhyme on the dāl. Whoever reads with the shaddah derives it from their saying: "nidd fulan" (the equal of so-and-so), and "nidd al-ba'ir" (the camel bolted) when it fled in its direction. This is supported by His words: ﴿The day you turn back in retreat﴾ and His words: ﴿The day a man flees from his brother﴾ [‘Abasa: 34]. Abu 'Ali said: the meaning of the speech is: indeed I fear for you the punishment of the day of calling out. al-Dahhak said: when people hear the roaring and groaning of Hell, they flee in terror into the earth, but they cannot head in any direction of the earth without seeing angels, so they turn back to where they came from. Others said: they are driven toward the Fire and flee, but they have no protector. As for the light recitation (tahfif), it is from "nida'" (calling out), and there are four opinions among the exegetes regarding it.

The first: at the blast of terror, people call out to one another. Abu Hurayrah related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, commands Israfil to blow the first blast, and he says: I shall blow the blast of terror. So the inhabitants of the heavens and the earth are terrified, except whom Allah wills. The mountains move, the earth quakes, nursing mothers are distracted, pregnant women miscarry, and people turn their backs fleeing, calling out to one another [and this is His words: ‘The day of calling out’]."

The second: it is the calling out of the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire to one another, as mentioned in [al-A'raf: 44, 50]. This is the view of Qatadah.

The third: it is their saying: "Alas for our regret! Alas for our destruction!" This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

The fourth: on that day every people will be called with their leader, with the happiness of the blessed and the misery of the wretched.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿The day you turn back in retreat﴾. There are two opinions regarding this. The first: fleeing from the Fire. The second: their being turned back toward the Fire.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿You will have no protector from Allah﴾, that is, no preventer.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And Joseph had certainly come to you before﴾. This is Joseph son of Jacob. It is said that this is not him, and this is not correct.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Before, with clear proofs﴾, which are the indications of monotheism, like His words: ﴿Are separate lords better, or Allah, the One, the Irresistible?﴾ [Yusuf: 39]. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: the clear proofs were the interpretation of dreams and the splitting of the shirt. It was also said: rather, Allah sent him after the death of the king of Egypt to the Copts.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿You remained in doubt about what he brought you﴾, that is, of worshipping Allah alone, ﴿until, when he died﴾, that is, passed away, ﴿you said: "Allah will never send after him a messenger."﴾ That is, you persisted in your disbelief and assumed that Allah would not renew the proof against you. ﴿Thus﴾ [p. 222], that is, in this same error ﴿Allah leads astray whoever is a transgressor﴾, that is, a polytheist, ﴿a doubter﴾, that is, one who is in doubt about monotheism and disbelieves the messengers.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿You remained in doubt about what he brought you﴾, that is, of worshipping Allah alone, ﴿until, when he died﴾, that is, passed away, ﴿you said: "Allah will never send after him a messenger."﴾ That is, you persisted in your disbelief and assumed that Allah would not renew the proof against you. ﴿Thus﴾ [p. 222], that is, in this same error ﴿Allah leads astray whoever is a transgressor﴾, that is, a polytheist, ﴿a doubter﴾, that is, one who is in doubt about monotheism and disbelieves the messengers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 40, verses 26–34:

﴿And Pharaoh said, "Leave me to kill Moses."﴾ He only said this because among Pharaoh's close associates there were those who would prevent him from killing Moses, out of fear of destruction. ﴿And let him call upon his Lord﴾, the one whom he claims has sent him; let Him protect him from being killed. ﴿Indeed, I fear that he will change your religion﴾, meaning your worship of me, ( ﴿and that he will cause corruption to appear in the land﴾ ). Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "wa-an" without an alif. 'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "aw an" with an alif before the waw, meaning: if he does not change your religion, he will cause corruption. However, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr read "yuzhira" with a damma on the yā' and "al-fasad" in the accusative (naṣb). The rest read "yazhara" with a fatha on the yā' and "al-fasadu" in the nominative (raf'). The meaning is: corruption will appear through the alteration of our laws, so he deemed that corruption according to his own claim. It was also said: he will kill your sons as you do to them.

When Pharaoh said this, Moses sought refuge with his Lord, and said: ﴿Indeed, I have sought refuge in my Lord and your Lord﴾. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "'udtu" with the dhāl clearly pronounced; Abu 'Amr, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far and Khalaf assimilated it (idghām). ﴿From every arrogant one﴾, meaning one who is too proud to believe. Pharaoh then intended to kill Moses, and at that point ﴿a man of faith from the family of Pharaoh said...﴾ [p. 217] There are two opinions regarding "al" (family) here.

The first: it means relatives and kin. As-Suddi and Muqatil said: he was a cousin of Pharaoh, and this is the one meant by the words: ﴿And there came a man from the farthest end of the city, running﴾ [al-Qasas: 20].

The second: it means clan and tribe. Qatadah and Muqatil said: he was a Copt. Some said: he was an Israelite, and the meaning is only: a man of faith who concealed his faith from the family of Pharaoh. Regarding his name there are five opinions.

The first: Hizbil, said by Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil. The second: Habib, said by Ka'b. The third: Sam'un, with an unpointed sīn, said by Shu'ayb al-Jiba'i. The fourth: Jibril (Gabriel). The fifth: Sham'an, with a pointed shīn, related from Ibn Ishaq; al-Zajjaj also related it as "Sham'an" with a shīn, and Ibn Makula mentioned it with a pointed shīn as well. Most scholars hold that he believed in Moses when Moses came. al-Hasan said: he was a believer before Moses came, and so was Pharaoh's wife. Muqatil said: he concealed his faith from Pharaoh for a hundred years.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Will you kill a man merely because he says, "My Lord is Allah"?﴾ That is, because he says ﴿"My Lord is Allah"﴾. This is a rhetorical question of denunciation. ﴿And he has certainly brought you clear proofs﴾, that is, things that indicate his truthfulness. ﴿And if he is a liar, upon him is his lie﴾, that is, that will not harm you. ﴿And if he is truthful, some of what he promises you will befall you﴾ of punishment. Regarding "some" (ba'd) there are three opinions.

[p. 218] The first: it means "all"; this was said by Abu 'Ubaydah, who cited the verse of Labid:

"Abandoner of dwelling places when I do not find them pleasing, or when some souls are seized by their death..."

He meant: all souls.

The second: it is redundant (ṣilah), and the meaning is: what he promises you will befall you. This is related from al-Layth.

The third: it retains its original sense, and there are two views on this. One: he promised them salvation if they believed and destruction if they disbelieved, so mention of "some" was used because they would be in one of the two states. The second: he promised them destruction in this world and punishment in the Hereafter for their disbelief, so their destruction in this world became part of the promise. Both are mentioned by al-Mawardi.

Al-Zajjaj said: this is a method of reasoning in which the debater binds the opponent to the proof using the least demanding aspect of the matter, and this does not negate that all of it will befall them. A similar statement is the poet's:

"The one who takes his time may attain some of his need, and the hasty one may well stumble."

The poet mentioned "some" only to imply the whole, because "some" is part of the whole. But when the speaker says: the least that the patient one gains is attaining some of his need, and the least that the hasty one gets is stumbling, he has shown the superiority of the patient over the hasty by something the opponent cannot refute. Thus the believer was saying to them: at the very least, in his truthfulness, some of what he promises you will befall you, and in some of that is your destruction. He said: as for Labid's verse, he meant by "some souls" only his own soul.

[p. 219] His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide﴾, that is, does not grant success to what is right, ﴿one who is a transgressor﴾. There are two opinions regarding this. The first: he is the polytheist, said by Qatadah. The second: he is one who sheds blood unlawfully, said by Mujahid.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿Dominant in the land﴾, that is, exalted in the land of Egypt. ﴿So who will help us﴾, that is, who will protect us ﴿against the might of Allah﴾, that is, against His punishment. The meaning is: do not expose yourselves to punishment by denying him and killing the Prophet. At that point Pharaoh said: ﴿I show you only what I see﴾ of opinion and advice ﴿and I guide you only to the path of right conduct﴾, that is, I call you only to the way of guidance in denying Moses and believing in me. This indicates that he fell silent in response to the believer.

﴿And the one who believed said: "O my people, indeed I fear for you a day like the day of the factions"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, like the day of the faction of the factions; the meaning is: I fear that if you persist in your disbelief, punishment will come upon you like what befell the nations that denied their messengers.

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib, Ibn Jubayr, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Dahhak read "al-tannaddu" with the dhāl shaddah. Al-Zajjaj said: as for keeping the yā', that is the original form, and omitting it is good and fine, [p. 220] because the kasra indicates the yā', and it is the end of the verse, and the endings of these verses rhyme on the dāl. This is supported by His words: ﴿The day you turn back in retreat﴾ and His words: ﴿The day a man flees from his brother﴾ [‘Abasa: 34]. Abu 'Ali said: the meaning of the speech is: indeed I fear for you the punishment of the day of calling out. al-Dahhak said: when people hear the roaring and groaning of Hell, they flee in terror into the earth, but they cannot head in any direction of the earth without seeing angels, so they turn back to where they came from. Others said: they are driven toward the Fire and flee, but they have no protector. As for the light recitation (tahfif), it is from "nida'" (calling out), and there are four opinions among the exegetes regarding it.

The first: at the blast of terror, people call out to one another. The third: it is their saying: "Alas for our regret! Alas for our destruction!" This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

The fourth: on that day every people will be called with their leader, with the happiness of the blessed and the misery of the wretched.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿The day you turn back in retreat﴾. There are two opinions regarding this. The first: fleeing from the Fire. The second: their being turned back toward the Fire.

The explanation of the meaning of "jabbar" (tyrant, compeller) has already passed in [Hud: 59]. Abu 'Amr read "upon every heart" with tanwin (ʿalā kulli qalbin), while the rest of the seven readers read it with the idafa (ʿalā kulli qalbi). Abu 'Ali said: the meaning is: He seals the whole heart of the arrogant person. Al-Zajjaj chose the reading with the idafa, saying: because the arrogant one is the person, not the heart.

If it is said: if this reading were more correct, would the heart have been placed before "every"?

The answer: this is permissible among the Arabs. Al-Farra' said: placing this before that or after it is the same. I heard some Arabs say: "He combs his hair every Friday," meaning "every Friday," and the meaning is the same. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read "upon the heart of every arrogant one," placing the heart first.

The exegetes said: when the believer admonished Pharaoh and restrained him from killing Moses, Pharaoh said to his minister: ﴿O Haman, build me a tower﴾, which we have mentioned in [al-Qasas: 38].

Abu 'Ali said: the meaning is: He seals the whole heart of the arrogant person. Al-Zajjaj chose the reading with the idafa, saying: because the arrogant one is the person, not the heart.

If it is said: if this reading were more correct, would the heart have been placed before "every"?

The answer: this is permissible among the Arabs. Al-Farra' said: placing this before that or after it is the same. I heard some Arabs say: "He combs his hair every Friday," meaning "every Friday," and the meaning is the same. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read "upon the heart of every arrogant one," placing the heart first.

The exegetes said: when the believer admonished Pharaoh and restrained him from killing Moses, Pharaoh said to his minister: ﴿O Haman, build me a tower﴾, which we have mentioned in [al-Qasas: 38].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That I may reach the ways﴾ ﴿the ways of the heavens﴾. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada said: it means its gates. Abu Salih said: its paths. Others said: the meaning is: that I may reach the routes from one heaven to another. Al-Zajjaj said: that I may reach whatever leads me to the heavens. What follows this is explained in [al-Qasas: 38], up to His saying: ﴿And thus﴾, that is, like what We have described, ﴿the evil of his deed was made attractive to Pharaoh, and he was barred﴾ from the path of guidance. Asim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "wa-Suddu" with a damma on the sad, while the rest read it with a fatha. ﴿And the plot of Pharaoh﴾ against the signs of Moses ﴿was only in ruin﴾, that is, in futility and loss.

(p-224) Then the discourse returned to the believing man's admonition to his people, which is his saying: ﴿Follow me; I will guide you to the path of right conduct﴾, i.e., the path of guidance. ﴿O my people, this worldly life is but a passing enjoyment﴾, meaning that life in this abode is an enjoyment one savors for a few days, then it ends. ﴿And indeed, the Hereafter is the abode of settlement﴾, which has no cessation.

﴿Whoever does an evil deed﴾: there are two views concerning it. The first is that it is polytheism (shirk), and like it is Hell; this is the view of most scholars. The second is that it refers to sins, and like it is the punishment commensurate with them; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi. According to the first view, the righteous deed is monotheism (tawhid); according to the second, it is [upon] general application.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then those will enter Paradise﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "yudkhalūna" with a damma on the yā' (yudkhalūna). Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited it with a fatha. From 'Asim, both readings are reported.

Regarding His saying: ﴿without reckoning﴾, there are two views. The first is that there will be no accountability for them concerning what they are given in Paradise; this was said by Muqatil. The second is that He will pour provision upon them in abundance, without restriction; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

O my people, what is the matter with you that I call you to salvation, while you call me to the Fire? That is, what is the matter with you? It is like saying, "What is the matter with me that I see you sad?" The meaning of the verse is: tell me, what is this state? I call you to salvation from the Fire through faith, while you call me to the Fire, that is, to polytheism, which necessitates the Fire. Then he explained the two calls in what follows.

The meaning of ﴿I have no knowledge of it﴾ is: I do not know this that you claim as a partner to Him. What follows has already been explained (Al-Baqarah 2:129; Ta Ha 20:82), up to His words ﴿has no call﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: it has no answered call, as stated by al-Suddi. The second: it has no intercession, as stated by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His words ﴿and that our return is to God﴾ mean: our return (marji'), and the meaning is that He will requite us for our deeds. Regarding "the transgressors" (al-musrifin) there are two views, which we have mentioned at His words ﴿a transgressor, a liar﴾ (Ghafir 40:28).

His words ﴿You will remember what I say to you﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-'Aliyah, Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and Abu Raja' read ﴿فَسَتُذَكَّرُونَ﴾ with a fatha on the dhal and a lightened form, and with a shadda and fatha on the kaf. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani read it with a fatha on the dhal and kaf and shadda on both. The meaning: when the punishment comes down upon you, you will remember what I said to you in the world of counsel.

﴿And I entrust my affair to God﴾, that is, I refer it (to Him). This was because they had threatened him for opposing their religion. ﴿Indeed God is Seeing of the servants﴾, that is, of His friends and His enemies.

Then the believer left them, and they sought him but could not reach him. He was saved along with Moses when he crossed the sea. This is His words: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they schemed﴾, that is, from the harm they intended for him. ﴿And there befell the people of Pharaoh﴾, when they were drowned in the sea, ﴿the worst of punishment﴾. The exegetes said: it is drowning.

His words: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening.﴾ Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas said: the spirits of the people of Pharaoh are in the bellies of black birds, and they are exposed to the Fire twice each day, and it is said: "O people of Pharaoh, this is your abode."

Ibn Jarir narrated, saying: 'Abd al-Karim ibn Abi 'Umayr narrated to us, saying: Hammad ibn Muhammad al-Balkhi narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Awza'i, and a man asked him, saying: "We have seen birds coming out of the sea and taking the direction of the west, white, in flocks upon flocks, whose number none knows but God; and when evening comes, the like of them returns black." He said: "And have you noticed this?" He said: "Yes." He said: "Indeed those birds have in their crops the spirits of the people of Pharaoh, who are exposed to the Fire morning and evening. So they return to their nests with their feathers burnt and blackened, and white feathers grow on them by night, while the black ones fall away. Then they go out in the morning, and they are exposed to the Fire morning and evening, [then they return to their nests]. That is their custom in the world. And when the Day of Resurrection comes, God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Admit the people of Pharaoh into the severest punishment﴾."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim in their two Sahihs narrated from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When one of you dies, his seat is shown to him morning and evening: if he is one of the people of Paradise, then [it is] of the people of Paradise; and if he is one of the people of the Fire, then [it is] of the people of the Fire. It is said: 'This is your seat, until God resurrects you to it on the Day of Resurrection.'"

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, [Abu 'Amr], Abu Bakr and Aban from 'Asim read ﴿السّاعَةُ ادْخُلُوا﴾ with a damma, and a damma on the kha', in the sense of a command to them to enter. The beginning, according to the reading of these, is with a damma on the alif. The rest read with a hamza of cutting (qat') and a kasra on the kha', in the sense of a command to the angels to admit them; and these begin with a fatha on the alif.

And when the Day of Resurrection comes, God, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Admit the people of Pharaoh into the severest punishment﴾."

Al-Bukhari and Muslim in their two Sahihs narrated from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "When one of you dies, his seat is shown to him morning and evening: if he is one of the people of Paradise, then [it is] of the people of Paradise; and if he is one of the people of the Fire, then [it is] of the people of the Fire. It is said: 'This is your seat, until God resurrects you to it on the Day of Resurrection.'"

This verse indicates the punishment of the grave, because He clarified what awaits them in the Hereafter, saying: ﴿And the Day the Hour arises: Admit...﴾. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, [Abu 'Amr], Abu Bakr and Aban from 'Asim read ﴿السّاعَةُ ادْخُلُوا﴾ with a damma, and a damma on the kha', in the sense of a command to them to enter. The beginning, according to the reading of these, is with a damma on the alif. The rest read with a hamza of cutting (qat') and a kasra on the kha', in the sense of a command to the angels to admit them; and these begin with a fatha on the alif.

O my people, what is the matter with you that I call you to salvation, while you call me to the Fire? That is, what is the matter with you? It is like saying, "What is the matter with me that I see you sad?" The meaning of the verse is: tell me, what is this state? I call you to salvation from the Fire through faith, while you call me to the Fire, that is, to polytheism, which necessitates the Fire. Then he explained the two calls in what follows.

The meaning of ﴿I have no knowledge of it﴾ is: I do not know this that you claim as a partner to Him. What follows has already been explained (Al-Baqarah 2:129; Ta Ha 20:82), up to His words ﴿has no call﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: it has no answered call, as stated by al-Suddi. The second: it has no intercession, as stated by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His words ﴿and that our return is to God﴾ mean: our return (marji'), and the meaning is that He will requite us for our deeds. Regarding "the transgressors" (al-musrifin) there are two views, which we have mentioned at His words ﴿a transgressor, a liar﴾ (Ghafir 40:28).

His words ﴿You will remember what I say to you﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-'Aliyah, Abu 'Imran al-Jawni and Abu Raja' read ﴿فَسَتُذَكَّرُونَ﴾ with a fatha on the dhal and a lightened form, and with a shadda and fatha on the kaf. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani read it with a fatha on the dhal and kaf and shadda on both. The meaning: when the punishment comes down upon you, you will remember what I said to you in the world of counsel.

﴿And I entrust my affair to God﴾, that is, I refer it (to Him). This was because they had threatened him for opposing their religion. ﴿Indeed God is Seeing of the servants﴾, that is, of His friends and His enemies.

Then the believer left them, and they sought him but could not reach him. He was saved along with Moses when he crossed the sea. This is His words: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they schemed﴾, that is, from the harm they intended for him. ﴿And there befell the people of Pharaoh﴾, when they were drowned in the sea, ﴿the worst of punishment﴾. The exegetes said: it is drowning.

His words: ﴿The Fire; they are exposed to it morning and evening.﴾ Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas said: the spirits of the people of Pharaoh are in the bellies of black birds, and they are exposed to the Fire twice each day, and it is said: "O people of Pharaoh, this is your abode."

Ibn Jarir narrated, saying: 'Abd al-Karim ibn Abi 'Umayr narrated to us, saying: Hammad ibn Muhammad al-Balkhi narrated to us, saying: I heard al-Awza'i, and a man asked him, saying: "We have seen birds coming out of the sea and taking the direction of the west, white, in flocks upon flocks, whose number none knows but God; and when evening comes, the like of them returns black." Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 40, verses 47–52:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And [mention] when they will dispute within the Fire﴾. The meaning: Recount to your people, O Muhammad, when they (i.e., the people of the Fire) will argue with one another. The verse has been explained in [Surah] [Ibrahim: 21]. "Those who were arrogant" are the leaders. The meaning of ﴿Indeed, we are all within it﴾ is: we and you. ﴿Indeed, Allah has already judged between the servants﴾ means: He has decreed this against us and against you. As for the meaning of the guards of Hell saying to them: ﴿Then call upon [Him]﴾, it means: we do not call upon Him for you. ﴿And the supplication of the disbelievers is not but in error﴾, meaning: that supplication is void and does not benefit.

﴿Indeed, We will surely support Our messengers and those who believe in the worldly life﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions.

The first: that this is by establishing their proofs. The second: by destroying their enemies. The third: that the final outcome will be theirs. The decisive view is that their victory is certain and unavoidable: sometimes it is by elevating their cause, as He gave Dawud and Sulayman a kingdom with which they subdued every disbeliever, and He made Muhammad (ﷺ) prevail over those who denied him; sometimes it is by exacting vengeance upon their deniers by saving the messengers and destroying their enemies, as He did with Nuh and his people, and Musa and his people; and sometimes it is by exacting vengeance upon their deniers after the messengers' death, as when He gave Bukhtunassar power over the killers of Yahya ibn Zakariyya. As for their victory on the Day when the witnesses stand, Allah will save them from the punishment. The singular of al-ashhad (the witnesses) is shahid (witness), just as the singular of as-ashab (the companions) is sahib (companion). Concerning al-ashhad there are three opinions.

The first: the angels, who testified for the prophets that they conveyed the message and against the nations that they denied. This is the view of Mujahid and as-Suddi. Muqatil said: they are the angels who record deeds.

The second: the angels and the prophets; this is the view of Qatadah.

The third: they are four: the prophets, the angels, the believers, and the limbs; this is the view of Ibn Zayd.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The Day when their excuse will not benefit the wrongdoers﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr recited "tanfa'u" with the letter ta' (taa), while the rest recited it with the letter ya' (yaa); the reason being that "al-ma'dhira" (excuse) and "al-i'tharr" (apologizing) have the same meaning. ﴿Their excuse﴾: that is, it will not be accepted from them if they make excuses. ﴿And theirs is the curse﴾: that is, distance from mercy. We have already explained in [Al-Ra'd: 25] that "lahum" here means "alayhim" (upon them). ﴿And theirs is the evil home﴾: that is the Fire.

[p. 233] We gave Moses the guidance (*al-huda*) from misguidance, meaning the Torah, and We caused the Children of Israel to inherit the Book after Moses. According to most scholars, this Book is also the Torah. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: it is the Torah, the Gospel, and the Psalms. *Al-dhikra* means admonition.

﴿So be patient﴾ over their harm, ﴿for the promise of God is true﴾ regarding your victory. This verse appears in this surah in two places [Ghafir: 55, 77]. They have said that it was abrogated by the verse of the sword (*ayat al-sayf*, the verse commanding armed fighting). The meaning of "glorify" (*sabbih*) is: pray.

There are three opinions concerning the intended meaning of "the prayer of the evening and the morning" (*salat al-'ashiyy wa'l-ibkar*).

The first: they are the five daily prayers. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

[p. 234] The second: they are the dawn prayer and the afternoon prayer. This was said by Qatada.

The third: it is a prayer that was performed before the prayers were prescribed, two units (*rak'atan*) in the morning and two units in the evening. This was said by al-Hasan.

As for what follows this, it has been discussed earlier [Ghafir: 4], up to His saying: ﴿There is nothing in their breasts but pride...﴾. The verse was revealed concerning the Quraysh. The meaning is: what drives them to deny you is only the arrogance in their hearts toward you, and they will not attain what that pride seeks, because God will humiliate them. ﴿So seek refuge in God﴾ from their evil. Then He drew attention to His power by saying: ﴿The creation of the heavens and the earth is greater than the creation of mankind﴾, that is, than their re-creation, [p. 234 continued] because of the multitude of their parts and the greatness of their bulk. Thus He alerted them to His power to re-create creation. ﴿But most people do not know﴾, meaning the disbelievers, when they do not draw evidence from this for the Oneness of God.

Muqatil said: The Jews exalted the Dajjal (the Antichrist) and said: "Our companion will be sent forth at the end of time and he will have authority." God then said: ﴿Indeed, those who dispute concerning the signs of God﴾, because the Dajjal is one of His signs, ﴿without authority﴾, that is, without proof. So seek refuge in God from the trial of the Dajjal. He said: the intended meaning of "the creation of mankind" is the Dajjal. Abu al-'Aliyah took a similar view, but the first view is more sound.

What follows this is clear, up to His saying: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: "Declare My oneness and worship Me, and I will reward you." This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: "Ask Me, and I will give you." This was said by al-Suddi.

﴿Indeed, those who are too proud to worship Me﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: too proud to affirm My oneness. The second: too proud to call upon Me and ask Me. ﴿They will enter Hell, humbled.﴾ Ibn Kathir recited *sa-yudkhalūna* (with the first letter *ya* pronounced with a *ḍamma*, i.e., *sa-yudkhalūna*) [with the *ya* vowelled as *yu-*], and Abu Bakr from 'Asim and 'Abbas ibn al-Fadl from Abu 'Amr recited *sa-yudkhalūna* [with a *ḍamma* on the *ya*]; the rest recited it with a *fatḥa*. *Al-dakhir* means: the humiliated, the abased.

What follows this has already been discussed in several places [Yunus: 67; al-Qasas: 73; al-An'am: 95; al-Naml: 61; al-A'raf: 54, 29; al-Hajj: 5], up to His saying: ﴿And that you may reach a specified term﴾, which is the lifespan from life until death. ﴿And perhaps you will use reason﴾, to recognise God's Oneness and His power.

They say: "It is not from Allah." ﴿How are they turned away?﴾ That is: how have they been turned away from the truth to falsehood? There are two opinions concerning them. The first: they are the polytheists; this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The second: they are the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine predestination), as mentioned by a group of exegetes. Ibn Sirin used to say: "If it was not revealed concerning the Qadariyyah, then I do not know concerning whom it was revealed."

Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu Razin, Abu Mijlaz, al-Dahhak, Ibn Ya'mar and Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited: "wal-salasila yasbahun" (and the chains, they will be dragged), with a fatha on the lam and the ya'. Ibn 'Abbas said: "When they drag them, it is more severe upon them."

(p-237) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They will be burned in the fire (yusjarun)﴾. Mujahid said: "The fire will be kindled with them, so they become its fuel."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Where are those you used to associate [with Allah]?﴾ It is explained in [al-A'raf: 190].

Concerning His saying: ﴿We used to call upon nothing before﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: they meant that the idols were not anything, because they neither harmed nor benefited; this is the view of the majority.

The second: they said it in the manner of denial; this was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

﴿Thus﴾ that is: just as Allah misguided these, He misguides the disbelievers.

﴿That﴾ the punishment which has descended upon you is ﴿because you used to exult in the earth without right﴾, that is: in falsehood, ﴿and because you used to be insolent (tamrahun)﴾. We have explained insolence (al-maraḥ) in [al-Isra': 37]. What follows this has already been mentioned in full [al-Nahl: 29; Yunus: 109; al-Nisa': 164], up to His saying: ﴿And it was not for a messenger to bring a sign except by permission of Allah﴾. That is because they used to demand signs from him. ﴿So when the command of Allah comes﴾, which is His judgment between the prophets and their nations, and ﴿the falsifiers (al-mubtiluna)﴾ are the people of falsehood.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [that] you may reach upon them a need within your breasts﴾, that is: your needs in the lands.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So which of the signs of Allah do you deny?﴾ This is an interrogative of reproach.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So what availed them﴾. Concerning "ma" there are two opinions. The first: it is negative. (p-238) The second: [it is] interrogative; Ibn Jarir mentioned both.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They rejoiced in what knowledge they had﴾. Concerning those referred to there are two opinions.

The first: [they are] the disbelieving nations; this is said by the majority. Then, concerning the meaning of the statement, there are two opinions. The first: they said, "We are more knowledgeable than them; we will not be resurrected nor brought to account"; this was said by Mujahid. The second: they rejoiced in what they had, thinking it to be knowledge; this was said by al-Suddi.

The second opinion: they are the messengers; and the meaning is: the messengers rejoiced when the deniers were destroyed and they were saved, with the knowledge of Allah they had, when His confirmation came; this was related by Abu Sulayman and others.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there encompassed them﴾, meaning the deniers, ﴿the punishment they used to mock﴾. Ba's (al-ba's) means punishment. The meaning of ﴿the sunnah of Allah﴾ is that He established this practice among the nations, namely that their faith does not benefit them when they see the punishment. ﴿And the disbelievers were lost thereupon﴾.

(p-239) If it is said: "As if they were not losers before that?"

There are two answers to this. The first: "khasira" means "halaka" (perished); this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: He only made clear to them their loss at the descent of the punishment; this was said by al-Zajjaj.
